title: Restaurants & Eating Out
subtitle: Book a table, order a full meal with your dietary needs, and settle the bill like a local

lessons.title: Réserver une table
lessons.description: Phone a French restaurant, ask what is available and book a table with the polite formulas that native speakers actually use.

blocks.heading: Le coup de téléphone
blocks.body: A French restaurant answers the phone with the name of the place, so start by saying who you are and what you want. The two words that open every booking call are Bonjour and je voudrais. Then you give three pieces of information in the same order every time: how many people, which day, and what time. If the restaurant needs a moment, you will hear Ne quittez pas — literally "don't leave", meaning "hold the line".

examples.french: Bonjour, je voudrais réserver une table, s'il vous plaît.
examples.english: Hello, I'd like to book a table, please.

examples.french: Pour quatre personnes, samedi soir, vers vingt heures.
examples.english: For four people, Saturday evening, around eight o'clock.
examples.note: people → day → time, always in that order

examples.french: Ne quittez pas, je vérifie.
examples.english: Hold the line, I'm checking.

examples.french: C'est à quel nom ?
examples.english: What name is it under?
examples.note: the standard question — answer just with your surname

examples.french: Au nom de Martin, M-A-R-T-I-N.
examples.english: Under the name Martin, M-A-R-T-I-N.

examples.french: C'est noté, à samedi !
examples.english: That's noted down, see you Saturday!

blocks.tip: French restaurants serve in two sittings — le service de midi (roughly 12h–14h) and le service du soir (19h30–22h). Outside those hours the kitchen is closed, so always book inside a service.

blocks.heading: Complet, libre, disponible
blocks.body: Three adjectives tell you whether you can eat. Complet means fully booked, libre means free or unoccupied, and disponible means available. The restaurant will often offer you an alternative rather than a flat no, so listen for the little question at the end: ça vous convient ? — does that suit you?

examples.french: Je suis désolé, nous sommes complets ce soir.
examples.english: I'm sorry, we're fully booked this evening.

examples.french: Est-ce que vous avez une table de libre à vingt et une heures ?
examples.english: Do you have a table free at nine o'clock?
examples.note: une table de libre — the de is optional but very common

examples.french: Il nous reste une table en terrasse.
examples.english: We have one table left on the terrace.

examples.french: Vingt heures trente, est-ce que ça vous convient ?
examples.english: Half past eight — does that suit you?

examples.french: Oui, très bien, ça m'arrange même.
examples.english: Yes, that's fine, it actually suits me better.

examples.french: Nous n'avons plus rien avant vingt-deux heures.
examples.english: We have nothing left before ten o'clock.

blocks.heading: Préciser sa demande
blocks.body: Once the time is agreed you can add a preference. Say it with une table + preposition: en terrasse (on the terrace), près de la fenêtre (near the window), dans un coin calme (in a quiet corner). If the meal is for an occasion, mention it — French restaurants gladly bring out a dessert with a candle. And always finish the call with merci beaucoup, au revoir : hanging up without both is considered rude.

examples.french: Serait-il possible d'avoir une table en terrasse ?
examples.english: Would it be possible to have a table on the terrace?
examples.note: serait-il possible de + infinitive = the most polite request there is

examples.french: Nous préférons une table près de la fenêtre.
examples.english: We'd prefer a table near the window.

examples.french: La salle du fond est plus calme, elle est moins bruyante.
examples.english: The back room is quieter, it's less noisy.

examples.french: C'est pour fêter l'anniversaire de ma femme.
examples.english: It's to celebrate my wife's birthday.

examples.french: Est-ce que le restaurant est accessible en fauteuil roulant ?
examples.english: Is the restaurant wheelchair accessible?

examples.french: Merci beaucoup, au revoir !
examples.english: Thank you very much, goodbye!

blocks.tip: If your plans change, call back and cancel: annuler une réservation takes ten seconds and is expected. Many small restaurants only have twenty covers, so an empty booked table really hurts.

blocks.heading: Le conditionnel de politesse
blocks.body: French softens requests with the conditional. You already know je voudrais (I would like) — it is simply vouloir in the conditional. Build the others the same way: take the infinitive and add -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. Pouvoir and vouloir are irregular stems (pourr-, voudr-), aimer is regular (j'aimerais). Je veux une table sounds like an order; je voudrais une table sounds like a human being.

examples.english: I'd like to book for three people.

blocks.tip: Two safe ready-made openers cover almost every situation: Je voudrais… for what you want, and Est-ce que ce serait possible de… for what you are asking someone else to do.

blocks.heading: Trois façons de poser une question
blocks.body: On the phone you will hear all three French question forms. Intonation (Vous avez une table ?) is casual. Est-ce que (Est-ce que vous avez une table ?) is neutral and always safe. Inversion (Avez-vous une table ?) is the most formal and is what restaurant staff use with customers. Notice that in inversion the verb and the pronoun swap places and are joined by a hyphen.

examples.french: Vous avez de la place ce soir ?
examples.english: Do you have room this evening?
examples.note: intonation — casual but perfectly polite with vous

examples.french: Est-ce que vous servez encore à quatorze heures ?

blocks.tip: With je, avoid inversion — ai-je and puis-je sound bookish. Say Est-ce que je peux… instead.

passages.title: Un appel au Bistrot des Halles
passages.french:
— Bistrot des Halles, bonjour !
— Bonjour, je voudrais réserver une table pour samedi soir, s'il vous plaît.
— Bien sûr. Pour combien de personnes ?
— Nous serons cinq, et nous aimerions dîner vers vingt heures.
— Ne quittez pas, je vérifie… Je suis désolée, à vingt heures nous sommes complets.
— Ah, c'est dommage. Est-ce que vous avez quelque chose plus tard ?
— Il me reste une table à vingt et une heures, dans la salle du fond. Elle est très calme.
— Parfait, ça nous arrange. C'est pour fêter l'anniversaire de ma sœur.
— Très bien, je note. C'est à quel nom ?
— Au nom de Lemaire. Merci beaucoup et bonne journée !
passages.english:
"Bistrot des Halles, good morning!"
"Hello, I'd like to book a table for Saturday evening, please."
"Of course. For how many people?"
"There will be five of us, and we'd like to have dinner around eight."
"Hold the line, I'm checking… I'm sorry, at eight o'clock we're fully booked."
"Oh, that's a shame. Do you have anything later?"
"I have one table left at nine o'clock, in the back room. It's very quiet."
"Perfect, that suits us. It's to celebrate my sister's birthday."
"Very good, I'm noting it down. What name is it under?"
"Under the name Lemaire. Thank you very much and have a good day!"

lessons.title: Commander un repas
lessons.description: Read a French menu from entrée to dessert, order confidently and explain allergies or a vegetarian diet.

blocks.heading: La carte, le menu, la formule
blocks.body: Careful: le menu in French is not the list of dishes — that is la carte. Le menu (or la formule) is a fixed-price deal: two or three courses chosen from a short list. A French meal runs in three courses: l'entrée (the starter), le plat (the main course) and le dessert. Le plat du jour is today's special, usually chalked on a board.

examples.french: La carte, s'il vous plaît.
examples.english: The menu, please.
examples.note: you are asking for the list of dishes

examples.french: Je prends le menu à vingt-cinq euros.
examples.english: I'll take the twenty-five-euro set menu.

examples.french: Et comme dessert, une tarte aux pommes.
examples.english: And for dessert, an apple tart.
examples.note: comme + course is just as common as en

blocks.tip: Waiters take the order course by course and often ask Et comme boisson ? at the end. A carafe d'eau (tap water) is always free — you never have to buy bottled water.

blocks.heading: Commander poliment
blocks.body: You have three interchangeable openings: Je voudrais…, Je vais prendre… and Pour moi, ce sera… . If you cannot decide, ask the waiter — Qu'est-ce que vous me conseillez ? is a compliment, not a bother. For meat, the waiter will ask about la cuisson: saignant (rare), à point (medium) or bien cuit (well done).

blocks.heading: Régimes et allergies
blocks.body: Say what you cannot eat with je suis allergique à… or je ne mange pas de… . Remember that after a negative, du / de la / des all become de: je ne mange pas de viande. For a diet, the adjectives are végétarien (no meat or fish), végétalien / vegan (no animal products at all) and sans gluten. Adding c'est grave, hein — it's serious — makes staff take an allergy seriously.

blocks.tip: In France a written allergy card in French, shown to the waiter, is very effective — kitchens are used to them and will check with le chef.

blocks.heading: Du, de la, des — et « de » après une négation
blocks.body: To order an unspecified amount you need the partitive article: du (masculine), de la (feminine), de l' (before a vowel) and des (plural). Je voudrais du pain = I'd like some bread. The rule that trips everyone up: after a negative, all of them collapse into plain de (or d'). Je mange du fromage → Je ne mange pas de fromage. The same de appears after quantity words: un peu de, beaucoup de, un verre de.

examples.english: I'd like some fish and some vegetables.

blocks.tip: Exception worth remembering: after être the article does not change. Ce n'est pas du poisson, c'est du poulet.

blocks.heading: Le pronom « en »
blocks.body: En replaces a noun introduced by du / de la / des or by a number, so you don't repeat yourself. Vous voulez du vin ? — Oui, j'en veux. It goes directly before the verb, and if there was a number or a quantity, you keep it at the end: J'en prends deux. In the passé composé, en sits before the auxiliary: j'en ai pris deux.

examples.french: — Vous voulez du pain ? — Oui, j'en veux bien, merci.
examples.english: "Would you like some bread?" "Yes, I'd like some, thank you."

examples.french: — Il y a des desserts sans gluten ? — Oui, il y en a deux.

lessons.title: L'addition
lessons.description: Ask for the bill, split it, deal with a mistake or a cold dish, and understand how tipping really works in France.

blocks.heading: Demander l'addition
blocks.body: In France the waiter will not bring the bill until you ask — leaving it on the table early would be rude. Catch the waiter's eye and say L'addition, s'il vous plaît, or the slightly more polite Est-ce qu'on pourrait avoir l'addition ? The verb for settling up is régler or simply payer. Once you have paid, on peut y aller — you can go.

blocks.heading: Partager l'addition
blocks.body: Splitting is completely normal. On partage means we're splitting; chacun paie sa part means each person pays their share. If you want a strictly equal split, say on divise en trois. Waiters can often split the payment across several cards — ask Vous pouvez faire deux cartes ?

blocks.heading: Réclamer et laisser un pourboire
blocks.body: If something is wrong, describe the problem calmly with il y a un problème avec… or je crois qu'il y a une erreur. Use the imparfait to describe how the food was — le plat était froid — and the passé composé for what happened: nous avons attendu quarante minutes. As for tipping: le service est compris by law, so a tip is optional. People simply round up or leave one or two euros per person when the meal was good.

blocks.tip: A calm complaint usually gets a real fix: the dish reheated, taken off the bill, or a free coffee — un geste commercial. Shouting gets you nothing.

blocks.heading: Se plaindre : passé composé et imparfait
blocks.body: A complaint mixes two past tenses. Use the passé composé for the events — what happened, once: nous avons attendu, vous avez oublié, j'ai commandé. Use the imparfait to describe the state of things — how the food was: le plat était froid, la viande était trop cuite, il n'y avait pas de sauce. Getting this pair right makes a complaint sound reasonable instead of aggressive.

blocks.tip: Open with Excusez-moi and a soft verb — je crois que, il me semble que. Excusez-moi, je crois qu'il y a une erreur is heard as a question; C'est faux ! is heard as an attack.

blocks.heading: Trop, trop de, pas assez de
blocks.body: Trop means too much and goes straight before an adjective: trop cuit, trop salé, trop cher. Before a noun you need de: trop de sel, trop de sauce. The opposite is pas assez (not enough), which follows exactly the same pattern: pas assez chaud, pas assez de pain. The de never changes for gender or number — trop de frites, trop de sauce.

passages.title: Une erreur sur l'addition
passages.french:
— L'addition, s'il vous plaît !
— Voilà, messieurs-dames. Soixante-quatre euros.
— Excusez-moi, je crois qu'il y a une erreur. Nous n'avons pas commandé de dessert.
— Ah, vous avez raison, je vérifie… C'est la table douze, pardon.
— Il y a aussi un problème avec l'entrecôte : elle était trop cuite.
— Je suis vraiment désolé. Je l'enlève de l'addition, et le café est offert.
— C'est très gentil, merci beaucoup.
— Ça fera donc quarante-huit euros. Vous payez ensemble ou séparément ?
— Séparément, s'il vous plaît. Vous pouvez faire deux cartes ?
— Bien sûr. Et le service est compris, ne vous inquiétez pas pour le pourboire.
passages.english:
"The bill, please!"
"Here you are, ladies and gentlemen. Sixty-four euros."
"Excuse me, I think there's a mistake. We didn't order any dessert."
"Ah, you're right, let me check… That's table twelve, sorry."
"There's also a problem with the rib steak: it was overcooked."
"I'm really sorry. I'll take it off the bill, and the coffee is on the house."
"That's very kind, thank you very much."
"So that will be forty-eight euros. Are you paying together or separately?"
"Separately, please. Could you do it on two cards?"
"Of course. And service is included, don't worry about the tip."
